package_info.package_manager: N/A (malicious file delivered via email or web download)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects Windows systems with Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool)
package_info.why_malicious: The malicious .diagcab file exploits a 0day path traversal vulnerability in the Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT), allowing attackers to copy an executable to the Windows Startup folder, resulting in arbitrary code execution upon next system boot. This enables persistent malware installation without user consent.

execution_context.file_location: maliciously crafted .diagcab file (delivered via email or web download)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
A .diagcab file containing a path traversal payload that copies a malicious executable to the Windows Startup folder, e.g.,

<CommandLine>copy ..\..\..\..\..\..\..\..\AppData\Local\Temp\malware.exe C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\malware.exe</CommandLine>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the malicious .diagcab file, the MSDT process executes a command that abuses path traversal to copy a malicious executable into the Windows Startup folder, resulting in the malware being executed automatically on next system boot.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The .diagcab file is crafted to exploit a path traversal vulnerability, enabling unauthorized file writes to sensitive system locations, which is a common technique for establishing persistence.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal .diagcab files are used for legitimate diagnostics and troubleshooting, not for writing executables to the Startup folder or performing file system modifications outside their intended scope.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate .diagcab files may copy diagnostic logs or scripts to temporary folders for troubleshooting, but never to the Startup folder or using path traversal.
key_indicators: Use of path traversal sequences (..\..\) in file copy commands
Copying files to the Windows Startup folder
Presence of executable payloads within a .diagcab archive

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious .diagcab file with a path traversal payload to copy a malicious executable to the Startup folder.
attack_chain.leads_to: User receives and opens the malicious .diagcab file.

attack_chain.action: User opens the .diagcab file, triggering MSDT to process the payload and copy the malware to the Startup folder.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious executable is placed in Startup folder.

attack_chain.action: On next system boot, Windows automatically executes the malware from the Startup folder, granting attacker code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and arbitrary code execution achieved.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of MSDT with .diagcab files containing path traversal sequences
Unexpected file writes to the Windows Startup folder by MSDT or child processes
Creation of new executables in Startup folder following .diagcab file opening
file_indicators: Presence of .diagcab files with embedded path traversal in command payloads
Temporary files in AppData\Local\Temp\ related to recent .diagcab activity
network_indicators: N/A (primary attack is local file system exploitation; follow-on malware may initiate C2 communications)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for .diagcab files containing suspicious command payloads with path traversal, and alert on any process (especially MSDT) writing executables to the Windows Startup folder. Correlate user activity with the opening of .diagcab files and subsequent creation of new autorun entries. Use endpoint protection to block or sandbox .diagcab files from untrusted sources.
